title: Validating-yet-balancing interpersonal advice framing
description: This latent fires on sentences in relationship/advice contexts that use a hedged, validating-but-balancing rhetorical move—phrases like 'it's important/essential/reasonable to recognize/understand/acknowledge'—to affirm one party's feelings or rights while simultaneously nudging consideration toward another perspective or need. It activates on empathetic, therapist-style statements that legitimize a boundary, desire, or motivation and then pivot to a caveat or competing consideration (someone else's feelings, one's own needs, hidden motivations). It would not activate on purely factual statements, direct commands, or advice that only takes one side without the balancing/acknowledging pivot, nor on emotionally neutral or unrelated topic sentences lacking this validating-hedge structure.

title: Announcing a balanced take before giving it
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic preamble phrases where the speaker signals that they are about to offer advice, an opinion, or a verdict, typically framing it as neutral, balanced, or nuanced (e.g., 'I'll try to provide a balanced perspective', 'Here's my take:', 'I'm going to give you my two cents', 'Let's break it down', 'So, AITA?'). It activates most strongly on these stock meta-commentary or scene-setting utterances themselves, rather than on the substantive content of the advice that follows. It does not activate strongly on sentences that actually deliver the reasoning, judgment, or evaluative content (e.g., 'You're not the asshole for having the pictures', 'It's essential to consider your daughters' feelings'), even though those sentences may occur in the same advice-giving context -- the latent is specifically tied to the introductory/announcing framing move, not the opinion itself.

title: Mindfulness/self-care advice list items
description: This latent fires on imperative-style bullet points recommending mindfulness, meditation, relaxation, or self-care practices, typically as items in a numbered or bulleted self-help list (e.g., 'Practice mindfulness**: ...', 'Try meditation, deep breathing, or yoga...'). It activates most strongly on the bolded action-verb lead-in itself ('Practice', 'Try', 'Learn', 'Take') paired with mindfulness/relaxation/gratitude content, and more weakly on related coping-strategy suggestions and self-care framing elsewhere in the text. It does NOT activate on general reflective or advice-giving prose that discusses emotions, relationships, or self-improvement conceptually without the imperative 'practice X technique' list format, nor on questions, explanations, or narrative commentary even if topically about coping or well-being.

title: Introducing an enumerated list
description: This latent fires on the boilerplate transition phrase that introduces a numbered or bulleted list of points, such as 'Here are some points to consider:' followed by the start of item 1 with bold formatting. It activates specifically on this list-preamble structure and the initial numbering/markdown markup ('1. **'), rather than on the substantive content of the list items themselves. It captures a formatting/discourse-structuring pattern common in assistant-style responses that organize information into enumerated points. It would not activate on prose that lacks this list-introduction framing, on list items deep into a list without the preamble, or on lists introduced differently (e.g., without the 'points to consider' phrasing or without bold numbering).

title: Suggesting assistance resources
description: This latent fires on list items or bolded headers that recommend concrete resources, programs, or services someone could seek out—government assistance, non-profits, job boards, scholarships, training programs, food banks, etc. It activates most strongly on short, formulaic 'Category: description' or bullet-style entries that name a specific type of aid or referral (e.g., 'Government assistance', 'Job search platforms', 'Local non-profit organizations') as part of an enumerated advice list, often for someone in financial, housing, employment, or medical need. It does not activate on general advice, reflective questions, emotional support statements, or interpersonal/relationship guidance that lacks a pointer to an actual assistance program or resource, even if such sentences appear in similarly structured numbered lists. The key trigger is naming or pointing to an external resource/program/service one can contact or apply to, not merely giving advice.

title: Social conversation-starting advice
description: This latent fires on advice-giving sentences that instruct the reader on how to initiate or build social/romantic connections, especially bolded imperative headers like 'Start with small talk', 'Find common ground', 'Show genuine interest', 'Use humor', and follow-up phrases like 'This can be a great way to start a conversation and build a connection.' It activates most strongly on formulaic listicle-style tips about small talk, shared interests, body language, smiling/eye contact, and breaking the ice, typically phrased as bolded strategy labels followed by brief elaboration. It does not activate (or activates weakly) on general relationship advice about conflict, boundaries, emotional support, or reflective/empathetic commentary that lacks the specific 'how to start/build a conversation or connection' framing, even if the topic is still interpersonal (e.g., sentences about coping with loneliness, respecting privacy, or handling disagreements).

title: Empathetic check-in questions
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic conversational openers used by an empathetic listener (e.g., a counselor or supportive interlocutor) to invite someone to share more about their feelings or situation, such as 'Is everything okay?', 'What do you think?', and 'Can you tell me more about what's been going on?'. It activates most strongly on these stock phrases themselves, especially when they appear as standalone or near-verbatim questions, and even on truncated fragments like 'Can' or 'What do you' that are clearly the start of such a question. It activates more weakly on longer, content-rich advice or reflective statements that merely paraphrase or extend the same solicitous, check-in intent (e.g., 'Is there anything you're worried about...'). It would not activate on declarative statements, factual explanations, or advice-giving sentences that don't take the form of a direct, open invitational question to the listener.

title: Empathetic exclamatory validation openers
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory phrases that validate or affirm the listener's feelings or situation, typically as a standalone reaction opener in an advice/support-style response (e.g., "That's wonderful!", "That's completely understandable!", "That's a great feeling!", "That can be a really tough and frustrating feeling."). It activates most strongly on brief, punchy, template-like affirmations that begin with "That's" or "That can be" and immediately label an emotion or situation as positive, normal, or difficult, often followed by an exclamation point. It activates more weakly on longer, more elaborated empathetic or validating sentences embedded in fuller explanations (e.g., "It's understandable that you're feeling upset and neglected given the circumstances"). It does NOT activate on sentences that give advice, ask questions, describe a situation neutrally, or express empathy through longer discursive reasoning rather than a short exclamatory validation phrase.

title: Highlighting relational impact/consequences
description: This latent fires on sentences that point out how one person's behavior or decision affects another person or their relationship, typically in an advice-giving or interpersonal-reasoning context. It activates on statements that shift focus from a described action to its consequences for a relationship, time, bonding, or emotional dynamic between people, often using phrases like 'the impact on' or 'taking up her time.' It is not simply about describing an action or event itself, nor about abstract cause-and-effect reasoning in non-relational domains (e.g., physical or logical causation); it specifically targets the framing of interpersonal or relational consequences, often within advice or counseling-style discourse.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral token that begins an item in an enumerated list (e.g., '2.', '3.', '4.'), typically within advice-giving or reasoning text that breaks points into a numbered sequence. It activates most strongly on bare list-number tokens, often followed by bold formatting markers, and also fires more weakly on introductory phrases that precede such lists ('Here's why:', 'Consider the following:') or on standalone prose sentences that appear near list structures. It would not activate on ordinary prose sentences lacking any list enumeration, non-numeric bullet points, or numbers used in other contexts (dates, quantities, measurements) rather than as list markers.

title: Judging someone's reaction as disproportionate or unacceptable
description: This latent fires on evaluative verdict statements in AITA/relationship-advice style text that pass judgment on a person's emotional reaction or behavior, typically labeling it as unreasonable, disproportionate, aggressive, unfair, hostile, or unacceptable (e.g., 'Her reaction was disproportionate and unfair,' 'His tone was dismissive and aggressive'). It activates specifically on short, declarative sentences that name a subject (often a possessive like 'Her/His/The mom's reaction') and attach a negative evaluative adjective describing conduct or tone, frequently in template-like patterns ('X's reaction was Y and Z' or 'came across as W'). It does not activate on general advice-giving, hedged reassurance ('you're not the asshole'), open-ended questions, or descriptive/narrative sentences that merely recount events without explicitly evaluating someone's behavioral tone as excessive, rude, or improper.

title: Prioritization / precedence framing
description: This latent activates on language that signals one consideration should take priority over another, often in the context of weighing competing desires against goals or obligations (e.g., health goals overriding food cravings). It fires on phrases and sentences that explicitly frame a hierarchy of importance, concession language ('while it's understandable...'), or single words like 'Credit' that may cue attribution/priority concepts. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, purely descriptive content, or sentences that list options without asserting one should win out over another.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires most strongly on the bare numeral-plus-period tokens (e.g. '2.', '3.') that begin items in an enumerated list, especially within advice-style responses that break guidance into numbered steps or points. Its weaker, broader activation covers the surrounding sentences of such lists, which tend to be interpersonal/relationship advice about communicating calmly, setting boundaries, or apologizing. It is not simply about the topic of respectful communication; a sentence expressing the same advice in plain prose without list formatting, or a numeral used in a non-list context (e.g. as a quantity or date), would activate it far less or not at all.

title: Recommending seeking emotional support
description: This latent fires specifically on the stock advice-genre phrase telling someone to reach out to friends, family, or a therapist/counselor for emotional support and guidance, typically as a bulleted or standalone recommendation (e.g., 'Seek support:', 'Consider reaching out to...'). It activates most strongly on the canonical, near-templated wording of this suggestion, including fragments like 'Seek support.' or 'Consider' that are clearly truncated instances of the same template. It activates more weakly on related but distinct advice sentences in the same emotional-support context (e.g., self-care tips, validating someone's feelings, suggesting a specific conversation, or referencing a crisis hotline) that don't explicitly frame 'reach out/consider seeking support from friends/family/therapist' as the recommended action. It would not activate on general relationship advice, reflective statements, empathetic acknowledgments, or numbered-list scaffolding that lack this specific 'seek support from people around you or a professional' recommendation.

title: Proposing a compromise or negotiated solution
description: This latent fires on sentences that propose, suggest, or request a specific compromise, accommodation, or alternative arrangement to resolve an interpersonal conflict—often phrased as questions ('Could we...', 'Would you mind...', 'Maybe we could...', 'How about...') offering concrete options like taking turns, scheduling, splitting tasks, or finding a middle ground. It activates most strongly on direct, dialogue-style proposals suggesting mutual accommodation (chores, noise, time, money, space) between two parties. It does NOT activate on general advice, reflection, or third-person commentary about a situation (e.g., 'It's reasonable to expect...', 'You've done your part...') that doesn't itself constitute a proposed solution or negotiation offer, even if the topic is similar (conflict resolution, fairness, boundaries).

title: Affirming self-honesty about limitations
description: This latent activates on statements that validate or reassure the reader that acknowledging their own limits, boundaries, or shortcomings is an act of honesty rather than weakness or failure. It responds to reassuring, second-person framings that reframe self-awareness of limitations as a positive, authentic act ('you're simply being honest with yourself'). It would not activate on neutral descriptions of limitations themselves, factual statements about boundaries without an evaluative/reassuring framing, or third-person or abstract discussions of honesty unrelated to personal self-assessment.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on standalone numerals (with or without trailing period or bold markdown asterisks) that serve as the enumerator token beginning an item in a numbered list, such as '3.', '4.', or '2. **'. It activates most strongly on bare digit-plus-punctuation tokens in isolation, and more weakly when such markers appear alongside introductory list-preamble phrases like 'Here's an alternative approach:' or 'Here are some suggestions to consider:'. It would not activate on ordinary prose sentences, spelled-out numbers used in running text, or numbers that are not functioning as list-item delimiters (e.g., quantities, dates, or measurements embedded in a sentence).

title: Sentence-initial 'This can/might help...' framing
description: This latent fires on the specific syntactic template of a sentence beginning with a demonstrative pronoun ('This'/'It') followed by a modal helping verb ('can', 'might', 'will', 'could') and 'help', typically continuing into a positive relational outcome (diffuse tension, build trust, foster understanding, find a resolution). It activates most strongly on short, formulaic advice-summary sentences of this exact 'This can help...' construction, especially those following interpersonal-conflict advice in a chatbot response. It does not activate (or activates weakly) on sentences that express the same helpfulness idea but with different phrasing or subject (e.g. 'Communication is key', 'By setting boundaries you can...', 'It's essential to...'), nor on sentences that merely discuss relationships/communication without the 'This [modal] help' template, indicating the latent tracks this specific lexical-syntactic frame rather than the general topic of conflict resolution.

title: Plan disruption by another agent
description: This latent fires on sentences that frame a scenario where one party's intentions or plans are interfered with or derailed by another agent's actions. It activates on statements that establish a causal/relational structure of 'your plan' versus 'their disruptive action,' highlighting conflict or interference between agents' goals and outcomes. It is not simply about plans or actions in isolation, but specifically the framing of one agent's behavior undermining or disrupting another's intended course. Sentences that merely describe a plan without mention of interference, or describe unrelated actions without a disruptive causal link between two parties, would not activate it.

title: Age-old dilemma exclamation opener
description: This latent fires on short exclamatory phrases that frame an upcoming topic as a familiar, recurring dilemma, debate, or struggle—typically of the form 'The age-old/eternal [noun]!' used as a rhetorical lead-in before discussing an interpersonal or relationship problem. It activates most strongly on the exact templated phrase ('The age-old dilemma!', 'The age-old debate!', 'The eternal dilemma!') and variants naming the specific conflict (roommate drama, sibling rivalry, pizza debate), and activates more weakly on related but less formulaic framing exclamations ('The struggle is real!', 'What a tricky situation!', 'The eternal conundrum of...'). It would not activate on sentences that state advice, describe situations in narrative detail, or discuss the dilemma's content substantively without using this exclamatory 'age-old/eternal X!' framing device.

title: Reassuring affirmation of self-worth
description: This latent fires on direct, second-person affirming statements that reassure the reader of their worth, belonging, or capability, typically opening with imperative cues like 'Remember,' 'You are,' or 'You deserve' followed by validating content (e.g., 'you are enough,' 'you are not alone,' 'you deserve respect'). It activates most strongly on short, formulaic, emotionally supportive closing lines common in advice/therapy-style text, especially anaphoric repetitions of 'Remember' or 'You are/deserve' used as a comforting refrain. It does not activate on general advice-giving, empathetic acknowledgments of feelings, situational reasoning (e.g., 'It's essential to...', 'You did the right thing by...'), or third-person/explanatory sentences that discuss the person's situation rather than directly affirming their inherent worth or belonging in second person.
